title: Cop31 as it happened: EU and others reject deal as longest climate summit comes to fractious end
text:
So what happened today? Where to start? The conference officially finished on Friday, but on Saturday dragged on with continually shelved promises of a new draft cover text. In the evening, parties were told that there would be a plenary early on Sunday morning and to head out for the night.
The new texts were published during the night, and the wait for plenary began at 9am.
Before the plenary began, Germany said it would reject the current text.
Once in plenary, the EU officially objected to the cover decision, and other countries including Belize, Panama, Vanuatu, Norway and the UK joined them.
The summit ran into overtime and officially became the longest ever Cop.
The Cop president acknowledged that no agreement could be reached on the cover decision.
The breakdown of the talks were met with hurt and anger from all sides.
A number of other decisions, many of them procedural, were adopted, included on the Just Transition Mechanism.
In interviews after the breakdown, ‘Australia left nothing on the field,’ says Cop co-president Chris Bowen, and UN climate chief Simon Stiell admitted that consensus had fallen short.
If you want to read more analysis, my colleague Fiona Harvey has gathered together six key takeaways from the talks.
Thank you for reading the Guardian’s Cop live blog. See you next year …
Back in the UK there has been some reaction to an interview that the climate minister Miatta Fahnbulleh has done with the Sunday Times where she said: “[Rosebank’s oil] would be sold into global fossil fuel markets … We’re in the middle of an energy crisis where the conflict in the Middle East means that gas and oil prices are at record levels. That is the thing that’s impacting people’s bills. So if you care about how we’re going to drive down bills, it requires us to decouple ourselves from the global fossil fuel markets. And ultimately our way that we do that is through renewables, it’s through nuclear, it’s through clean energy.”
Responding for the Green Party, Carla Denyer, the environment spokesperson said: “Labour’s own energy secretary, in charge of making the decision on Rosebank, is being as clear as she can be this evening, that Rosebank would be a massive mistake, that it wouldn’t bring down domestic bills, and that if we are going to achieve this, we need to decouple ourselves from the domestic fossil fuel market. I hope she follows through with the right decision, for a safe future for all of us.”
The UK rejected the cover decision at Cop because it did not include reference to fossil fuels. Mohamed Adow, the founder and director of Power Shift Africa highlighted the issues of the government’s position: “The UK cannot wave through Jackdaw and Rosebank, then lecture the world about moving away from fossil fuels. That is rank hypocrisy. The UK is demanding ambition from others while giving the oil and gas industry permission to keep profiting from the climate crisis.
“The UK drilling for oil in the North Sea absolutely undermines its claims to be a climate leader.”
Now the delegate for Ethiopia, which will be hosting next years Cop, has stood up to speak: she says that today the world has been reminded “that multilateralism requires determination”.
“We are in difficult times but that difficulty is why Cop matters most … The UNFCCC remains the place where every country has a voice and where we come together to confront that challenge.”
She promises that the Cop in Addis Ababs will be the “Cop of hope … Hope for the young people who are risking what kind of world they will be living in, hope that despite our differences we can still come tgoether and have the most ambitious decision.”
He is followed onto the dais by the UNFCCC chief Simon Stiell, who spoke to reporters outside shortly before.
Stiell tells the plenary: “I share the disappoinment of many. Cop31 has been unable to agreee on both preseidency led decisions." Once again he emphasised where there has been progress. But, he said, “climate impacts are rising the world over. Fossil fuel costs are driving inflation the world over.”
“We’ve brought almost 200 countries together over two decades which have delivered results: climate targets, new goal and a goal on adaption.
“But there are lessons that must be learned… Consensus works best from ground up, with full transparency, taking time to listen to all views and building on what came before. There is clearly scope to improve, modernise and reform, not only because of what happend here but also because we must evolve.”
“This process has suffered setbacks before and come back stronger, it must do so again. Humanity can not afford anything else.”
The Cop president Murat Kurum has now resumed the plenary, opening it with a very sincere apology to the Ghana delegation who accused him of cutting them off earlier.
“Ghana is our friendly and brotherly country. I would like to ask their excellencies; such an attitude is by no means our attitude towards ghana and I have explained this to her. Again I’d like to apologise for the misunderstanding.”
The consensus system fell short today, concedes UNFCCC chief
Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UNFCCC, has just held a short press conference, where he emphasised that there had been many good outcomes of the conference but also acknowledged the issues.
Asked whether the consensus based system which broke down today when several countries refused to endorse the cover decision, he said: “That is the process we have, that is the process that got us through Paris and the progress made since, so it has worked.”
However, pressed further by a reporter who said that it may have worked in the past, but clearly did not work here, he conceded: “It certainly fell short today, but there are two stories to be told here.” He reminded reporters that this was a technical cop, and a significant number of the 160 agenda items were passed.
However, he said: “In terms of reform there has been a lot of discussion over the last couple years over the process … The conversation about how the process is to evolve moving forward is a live conversation.” And he said that he was engaging with parties around those challenging questions.
Lord Nicholas Stern, who wrote a landmark economic review of the impact of climate change for the UK government back in 2006, is searching for the positives. He points out that there were also positive developments in Turkey and says:
“We should now focus on the year ahead and work to strengthen shared commitment and to re-establish confidence in the multilateral process. We should remember that a valuable agreement was reached at the COP16 summit in Cancun, Mexico, in 2010 a year after disagreement in Copenhagen at COP15.
“The COP32 summit in Addis Ababa will provide a significant opportunity for the world to come together again to chart a new pathway for economic development and growth, particularly in Africa.”
Reaction to the failed cover decision and other key agenda points continues to pour in.
Ann Harrison, climate justice policy advisor at Amnesty International, said:
Countries from across regions were right to reject the colossal betrayal that the COP31 co-presidencies tried to pass off as climate action. They resisted a polluters’ charter designed to protect corporate profits while sacrificing people and the planet. They refused to accept a deeply unjust text that failed even to name fossil fuels while opening the door to risky technologies that could prolong their use.”
Mark Watts, executive director of C40 Cities, said:
This is one of the darkest hours in the history of climate negotiations and Cops cannot go on like this. The world needs braver leadership and urgent action. The era of overshoot has no room for failed climate diplomacy anymore. Every Cop must deliver collective action to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and address the most severe impacts of climate breakdown.
Today the Cop of Antalya failed to do that. The lack of courage by too many at Cop31 is not only undermining multilateralism, but, in the face of Super El Niño and worsening long-term climate conditions, it is costing lives.”
Teresa Anderson, the global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International, said:
Temperatures are rising, impacts are rising, but support for climate-hit countries is shrinking. The EU’s refusal to allow real progress on adaptation finance means that harvests will fail when they might have thrived. Buildings will collapse that could have withstood storms. People will drown because they didn’t get a flood alert. Millions of people will be left to deal with hunger, destruction and death that could have been avoided if rich countries cared about humanity’s future.
While the EU’s standing up to a text weak on fossil fuels has helped its reputation in this space, its self-appointed crown of climate leadership sits crookedly. The success of climate negotiations cannot be judged on carbon dioxide alone. Until wealthy polluting countries can stop seeing climate finance as a zero-sum game, climate talks will fail in their job of keeping humanity safe from rising temperatures.”
